# Living Project Documentation

Use this capability to find the document that settles a reader's engineering
question and keep its answer true as the project changes. A plan records
intent. Living documentation describes the behavior, constraints and
procedures that actually hold. Update their owning pages in place. In a Git
project, commits and pull requests carry the history of changes and checks.
The [OKF v0.3 specification](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/SPEC.md)
defines the bundle format. Here, `docs/` means the project's documentation root.

The requirement keywords used in this skill and its references follow
[RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.html).

## Organizing a bundle

See [documentation-structure.md](./references/documentation-structure.md) for:

- authoring an OKF v0.3 concept and distinguishing format requirements from this skill's discovery defaults
- choosing the subject that owns a decision, reviewing its page type, and routing readers from a subject index or glossary

See [conventions-and-operations.md](./references/conventions-and-operations.md) for:

- placing a team's engineering choice, an implementation guarantee or an architectural boundary
- tracing permission, activation, verification and recovery when several procedures share an authority

## Adopting or migrating documentation

See [bootstrapping.md](./references/bootstrapping.md) for:

- starting with a single reader question in a new project
- migrating an existing collection to OKF, including a tree that already passes validation, or carrying out an explicitly format-only request
- designing the layout from questions in handoffs and callers, checking each answer and its limits at the destination, and reporting the questions and checks still open

See [cross-references.md](./references/cross-references.md) for:

- settling support for published paths and fragments, updating callers and checking record identifiers
- making navigation work both inside the checkout and in an exported bundle

The [Scheduler example](./assets/docs-example/index.md) shows how readers enter through a subject, a familiar term or a deployment step and find the page that owns their decision. Its [rollback procedure](./assets/docs-example/operating/deployment.md#rolling-back) keeps the recovery command beside the condition that requires a restore.

## Consulting and maintaining docs

See [consulting-and-upkeep.md](./references/consulting-and-upkeep.md) for:

- consulting relevant owners before a plan and tracing dependent readers
- following a question from real entry points before and after a move, including the exception that changes the answer

See [validators.md](./references/validators.md) for:

- running one whole-root check for OKF conformance and engineering rules from the first day of migration
- interpreting evidence warnings and the editorial type list, using focused checks and qualifying a standalone export

3	## Detect before proposing
4	
5	“Adopt OKF for our engineering docs” calls for reviewing the populated
6	collection as it stands at checkout. Valid frontmatter can coexist with two
7	answers to the same question or a release command separated from its stop
8	condition.
9	
10	| Request                                          | Work and completion claim                                                                                                  |
11	| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
12	| Start a new or empty bundle                      | Answer the [first reader question](#start-with-a-reader).                                                                  |
13	| Migrate a populated root or package              | [Assess the collection](#assess-the-collection), design its subject layout, then migrate and verify the covered subjects.  |
14	| Add frontmatter only                             | Make the requested format changes and report the format checks. Leave the editorial outcome open.                          |
15	| Fix one page or keep docs current after a change | [Update affected claims and callers](./consulting-and-upkeep.md#find-the-affected-claim). Bound the result to that change. |
16	
17	**Guidelines:**
18	
19	- MUST identify the requested root or package, its entry points and its export boundary before interpreting the [whole-root check](./validators.md#check-the-whole-documentation-root).
20	- MUST preserve a working legacy layout until the project adopts migration. Follow its change gates, then carry an approved migration through to the owning pages and callers.

22	## Start with a reader
23	
24	One recurring question is enough to begin. For a new bundle the root index can
25	begin with this frontmatter, followed by a topic heading and a link to the
26	concept.
27	
28	```yaml
29	---
30	okf_version: "0.3"
31	title: Scheduler engineering
32	description: Job execution and delivery guarantees for Scheduler contributors.
33	---
34	```
35	
36	In a small library, the rest of that index can be a single link:
37	`[When will a failed job run again?](./retries.md)`. The whole bundle is
38	`index.md` and `retries.md`. The concept could read:
39	
40	```markdown
41	---
42	type: Specification
43	title: Job retries
44	description: Retry timing, attempt limits and the state callers observe between attempts.
45	---
46	
47	# Job retries
48	
49	A failed job waits one minute for a second attempt and appears as queued.
50	If the second attempt fails, the job ends as failed.
51	```
52	
53	Here the retry contract owns both timing and exhaustion. When readers also
54	need to count attempts, a growing project can group a Definition and a
55	Specification under scheduling. The [Scheduler subject index](../assets/docs-example/scheduling/index.md)
56	shows that choice in a larger service with its own retry limits. Link both
57	the human contributor guide and agent instructions to the same maintained
58	[placement convention](../assets/docs-example/contributing/documentation.md#choose-a-subject).

61	
62	- SHOULD answer the first question from the implementation or an adopted decision, give the answer a primary type, and link it from the index.
63	- SHOULD let a new decision earn its own page. Link it from the flat root or from the subject where readers already seek it.

66	
67	Start at the published root as someone who knows the product term but has
68	never seen this repository. Then try a caller with a narrower question, such
69	as a release operator arriving from a checklist. A contributor placing the
70	next related contract is another reader of the layout.
71	
72	Use actual questions from support handoffs, caller comments and maintenance
73	decisions. “What happens after cancellation **with an attempt still running**?”
74	can disappear if notes reduce it to “job lifecycle.” Keep the question and
75	its qualifying case in the working notes while reading the evidence. Against
76	each, leave room for the passage a reader can use, or the decision still open.

79	
80	- MUST inventory the initial tree across the requested scope. Include indexes, glossaries, human and agent entry points, external callers, tools and boundaries such as generated pages with a separate producer or immutable evidence.
81	- MUST [trace representative reader questions](./consulting-and-upkeep.md#verify-a-readers-route) in the existing collection before choosing a target layout. Carry every concrete in-scope question found during that assessment forward to a verified answer or an explicit gap.
82	- SHOULD scan every subject at page level in a large corpus, then inspect suspect sections and decision-critical routes closely. Look for mixed decisions, conflicting or repeated rules, unfamiliar terms, claims without support, questions without an owner and prerequisites stranded on other pages.
83

86	A root labeled “Specifications” and “Guides” asks a newcomer to predict
87	which kind of document contains the answer. A reader who asks when a job
88	becomes terminal can choose “Scheduling.” An operator deciding whether to
89	roll back can choose “Operating a release.” Try both routes in the
90	[worked Scheduler migration](../assets/scheduler-migration.md).

93	
94	- SHOULD sketch the smallest tree that answers the observed questions. Name each subject in the project's language and say which decisions it owns. Choose [page types and local indexes](./documentation-structure.md#choose-the-subject) once the owners are clear.
95	- SHOULD compare a minimal repair, such as a direct heading link, with a different grouping when ownership is ambiguous. Try a root lookup, [placing a new claim from a contributor entry point](./conventions-and-operations.md#contributor-routes) and the affected caller routes. Weigh the cost of maintaining old entries.
96	- MUST account for each affected legacy decision in working notes or the existing change record. Identify what stays, what moves or splits, which claims merge at one owner, and why a page is created or retired.
97	- MUST investigate missing answers in implementation, tests, configuration or an adopted decision. Write the rule and the case that distinguishes it from a plausible alternative at their owner. Where sources conflict or evidence runs out, tell the reader there what the source establishes, what remains unknown and which decision depends on it. A local observation may cover only one stage of a longer process.

99	## Migrate one reading route
100	
101	A metric's formula, its result-buffer contract and its presentation can change
102	independently. A sampled stage can compute values for several participants
103	while returning a score for only one. A caller needs the result Specification
104	to know whose score is available. By contrast, a configuration name, its
105	requiredness and its failure behavior together tell the operator what to set.
106	A testing convention and the counterexample that motivated it also belong
107	together.

110	
111	- MUST trace the slice's claims to their owners, callers, paths and fragments, exported assets, metadata and supporting evidence before editing.
112	- SHOULD split claims when they serve different decisions and can change independently. Keep facts that a reader must apply together on one page; page length and heading count alone do not justify a split.
113	- MUST carry each claim's limits, rationale and evidence into the typed owner, preserving established type names and existing metadata. Update generated material at its producer. Reconcile verified duplicates and retire obsolete material within the agreed scope.

A retained bookmark can serve external readers even after current instructions link straight to the owner. Update the subject index and glossary where readers use them.
115	- MUST preserve the action and any condition that changes it at the point of decision, including authority, cost, recovery or a safe no-op. Walk every offered recovery branch from the actual failure state. If a previous step already took effect, check what repeating it would change. Remove a fallback that contradicts the stop condition. Keep the ordered trace together when its sequence explains the outcome.
116	- MUST read each extracted page independently, exercise a boundary case and [trace the affected entry points](./consulting-and-upkeep.md#verify-a-readers-route) while its evidence is at hand. Do these reader checks even when format tooling is unavailable.
117	
118	## Close the requested scope
119	
120	In a flat library, a retry page can already answer both “When is the next
121	attempt?” and “What happens after the last one?” Opening that page from the
122	root and exercising exhaustion can justify keeping the layout. A local index
123	with only that destination would give the reader another step.
124

126	
127	- MUST reconcile the edited tree and working questions with the initial inventory. Open each recorded answer passage and answer the original question from that passage alone or its necessary links. Correct missing cases or record the gap. In the handoff identify covered subjects, remaining owners, unresolved questions and cross-package callers as applicable. Limit the completion claim to routes actually exercised.
128	- MUST report [format checks](./validators.md) separately from editorial results. Replay representative questions from the root and callers. For a repaired defect, show the original failure, the edited owner and the route to the complete answer. For a retained layout, identify a working owner, its boundary case and the detour an extra split or directory would introduce.
129	
130	## Preserve evidence identity
131	
132	An approval that names a file by SHA-256 binds to its bytes, including its first
133	line and newline convention. When retiring a dated feasibility study, move any still-useful check into the
134	operator's Procedure. Its next execution produces evidence for that change's
135	pull request. A reader investigating the old result can open the original
136	study at its commit.
137	
138	**Guidelines:**
139	
140	- MUST preserve any bytes an existing approval or distribution contract binds. If current guidance relies on that evidence, cite its pinned source and acceptance from the typed page that owns the claim. An existing Specification or Procedure can be its companion.
141	- MUST distinguish implemented behavior, an adopted target awaiting implementation, a revision-specific observation and an unverified hypothesis in the wording of the claim. 142	- SHOULD remove superseded reports from the live tree once active evidence obligations and reader routes are accounted for. Direct historical lookups to the original commit or pull request.
143	- MUST record hashes before migration and compare the exported evidence and linked assets byte-for-byte with their originals.
144	- MUST report intentional untyped evidence by path during verification so an accidental omission elsewhere remains visible.

1	# Documentation Structure
2	
3	## OKF v0.3 requirements
4	
5	OKF consumers discover typed concepts, assets and reserved navigation files
6	within one bundle. Untyped Markdown can coexist with concepts. The format
7	leaves the vocabulary open, so a consumer can encounter a type it has never
8	seen. See the [OKF v0.3 specification](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/SPEC.md).
9	
10	**Guidelines:**
11	
12	- MUST write a concept as UTF-8 Markdown with a YAML 1.2 core-schema mapping between lines containing exactly `---`. Its only universally required field is a nonempty string `type`. Keys must be unique.
13	- MUST reserve `index.md` and `log.md` at every depth. Nested indexes and logs have no frontmatter. An existing OKF log uses newest-first YYYY-MM-DD headings. Git-backed living docs use the commit history for changes. Leave the optional log out when bootstrapping.
14	- MAY declare `okf_version: "0.3"`, a title and a description on the root index. Preserve its existing frontmatter when refreshing the index.
15	- SHOULD edit only the metadata the change affects, preserving existing extension keys and values.
16	
17	## Choose the subject
18	
19	A parsing library can keep the accepted input and its error behavior under
20	parsing even when three modules implement it. Within a product, a capability
21	can own its history, sharing and platform-specific presentation. Move a common
22	interaction or terminology decision into shared design when independent
23	capabilities use it. A design system covers reusable foundations and components.
24	
25	**Guidelines:**
26	
27	- SHOULD start with the decision a reader brings and where they look for it. Choose the owning subject, then choose the page type by the claim it establishes.
28	- SHOULD distinguish caller guarantees, shared design, implementation, contributing, operations and authority where the readers and decisions differ. Use the project's names, package boundaries and depth.
29	- SHOULD record a [placement convention](./conventions-and-operations.md#contributor-routes) when contributors face a meaningful choice between subjects.
30	
31	## Engineering defaults
32	
33	These recommended types describe the decision the reader needs to make.
34	
35	| Type              | Reader's decision                                                    | What belongs together                                                                                                                     |
36	| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
37	| Definition        | Does this case count, and what does the value mean?                  | A metric's population, eligibility, units, formula and weighting.                                                                         |
38	| Specification     | Which observable outcome may a consumer rely on?                     | Inputs, results, timing, failure behavior and guarantees for each mode.                                                                   |
39	| Convention        | Which practice does the team use where several satisfy the contract? | The selected practice, its reason and the alternative it rules out. Lint enforcement leaves this a convention.                            |
40	| Architecture      | Who owns this responsibility, and how does work cross the boundary?  | Components, control or data flow and dependencies. Identify implemented boundaries, adopted targets and illustrative examples explicitly. |
41	| Procedure         | Who runs this task and how do they know it succeeded?                | Entry conditions, prerequisites, ordered actions, checks and recovery.                                                                    |
42	| Policy (optional) | Who may authorize this action or grant an exception?                 | Shared restrictions, exception authority and reopening conditions, when governed independently of any one procedure.                      |
43	
44	A table of configuration names, consumers and missing-value behavior can be a
45	single Specification when the reader needs those facts together.
46	
47	**Guidelines:**
48	
49	- SHOULD give each living page one primary type, a meaningful title and a short discovery description.
50	- SHOULD adopt the engineering vocabulary for a new bundle and preserve established project types and topic directories where readers or tools depend on them.
51	
52	### Review the declared type
53	
54	For each path in the validator's type list, write down the reader's question,
55	the claim this page owns and why the declared type helps the reader find that
56	claim. If answering requires several independent claims, identify the passages
57	and their owners. A project-specific name fits when readers use it for one
58	recognizable purpose and the page is maintained for that purpose.
59	
60	Try the [type-review example](../assets/type-review-example/index.md). Both
61	pages have valid type strings. An editor reading their content should reach
62	these decisions:
63	
64	| Page                                                          | Reader's question and the claim the page owns                                                                                                        | Editorial decision                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
65	| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
66	| [Notes](../assets/type-review-example/delivery-notes.md)      | How is the rate calculated? What does the API return for a zero denominator? What does the team do on Monday? Each answer can change independently.  | Flag the mixed `Description`. Put the formula in a Definition, the decimal or null return contract in a Specification, and the Monday reporting practice in a Convention. Link the pages where readers need to move between answers. |
67	| [Service registry](../assets/type-review-example/services.md) | Which team owns each production service today? The table owns the current service-to-team mapping and is updated as membership or ownership changes. | Accept `ServiceRegistry`. Readers can find the inventory by its established project type, and each entry answers the same question.                                                                                                  |
68	
69	## The index
70	
71	A scheduling index can list a Definition of retry limits beside the
72	Specification of what a client sees while waiting. A directory can contain
73	both. A root index can lead through nested indexes to either page.
74	
75	**Guidelines:**
76	
77	- SHOULD list concepts directly at the root while readers can select an answer there. Add a nested index when readers need to choose among a subject's subquestions. OKF permits a directory without an index.
78	- SHOULD link a subject index from its parent, state its scope and give each locally owned decision a descriptive route there. A caller with a specific question can link straight to the owning section.
79	- SHOULD keep rules at their typed owner and use indexes for navigation.
80	- SHOULD use Markdown links for index entries so OKF consumers can traverse them offline. An HTML link that works in a browser does not establish an OKF relationship.
81	- SHOULD add a page only when it owns an answer.
82	
83	## The glossary
84	
85	The legacy flat `specs/<domain>.md` convention pairs specs with glossary domain
86	headings. A typed Specification elsewhere creates no obligation to coin a term.
87	A glossary entry can link to a full Definition and still explain enough for a
88	reader to understand the word in context.
89	
90	For example, **Job output** names what one Job produced, even after its record
91	is gone. Three near-misses narrow or shift that meaning:
92	
93	| Candidate      | Likely interpretation       | Where it misleads                                          |
94	| -------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
95	| Output record  | A record that holds output  | Omits which job produced it.                               |
96	| Failure output | The output of a failed job  | Excludes successful jobs.                                  |
97	| Completed job  | An execution that has ended | Names the execution itself instead of what it left behind. |
98	
99	**Guidelines:**
100	
101	- SHOULD capture names from code, user-visible interfaces and team usage. Choose a new name whose ordinary meaning fits the concept. A plausible near-match hides the need to look it up.
102	- SHOULD use an optional cross-subject glossary for active aliases, UI labels and ambiguous terms. Give the minimum distinction, usually one to three sentences, and link to its owning section. Keep calculations, exceptions, procedures and guarantees at that owner.
103	- SHOULD explain a specialist term where its subject uses it. Group specialist terms in a subject-local Definition when readers consult them together.
104	- MUST account for every active alias and unique distinction when shortening a glossary, including meanings embedded in paragraphs. Move the distinction to an owner, retain a short finder or document the evidence for retirement in the change review.

# Documentation Structure

## OKF v0.3 requirements

OKF consumers discover typed concepts, assets and reserved navigation files
within one bundle. Untyped Markdown can coexist with concepts. The format
leaves the vocabulary open, so a consumer can encounter a type it has never
seen. See the [OKF v0.3 specification](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/SPEC.md).

**Guidelines:**

- MUST write a concept as UTF-8 Markdown with a YAML 1.2 core-schema mapping between lines containing exactly `---`. Its only universally required field is a nonempty string `type`. Keys must be unique.
- MUST reserve `index.md` and `log.md` at every depth. Nested indexes and logs have no frontmatter. An existing OKF log uses newest-first YYYY-MM-DD headings. Git-backed living docs use the commit history for changes. Leave the optional log out when bootstrapping.
- MAY declare `okf_version: "0.3"`, a title and a description on the root index. Preserve its existing frontmatter when refreshing the index.
- SHOULD edit only the metadata the change affects, preserving existing extension keys and values.

## Choose the subject

A parsing library can keep the accepted input and its error behavior under
parsing even when three modules implement it. Within a product, a capability
can own its history, sharing and platform-specific presentation. Move a common
interaction or terminology decision into shared design when independent
capabilities use it. A design system covers reusable foundations and components.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD start with the decision a reader brings and where they look for it. Choose the owning subject, then choose the page type by the claim it establishes.
- SHOULD distinguish caller guarantees, shared design, implementation, contributing, operations and authority where the readers and decisions differ. Use the project's names, package boundaries and depth.
- SHOULD record a [placement convention](./conventions-and-operations.md#contributor-routes) when contributors face a meaningful choice between subjects.

## Engineering defaults

These recommended types describe the decision the reader needs to make.

| Type              | Reader's decision                                                    | What belongs together                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Definition        | Does this case count, and what does the value mean?                  | A metric's population, eligibility, units, formula and weighting.                                                                         |
| Specification     | Which observable outcome may a consumer rely on?                     | Inputs, results, timing, failure behavior and guarantees for each mode.                                                                   |
| Convention        | Which practice does the team use where several satisfy the contract? | The selected practice, its reason and the alternative it rules out. Lint enforcement leaves this a convention.                            |
| Architecture      | Who owns this responsibility, and how does work cross the boundary?  | Components, control or data flow and dependencies. Identify implemented boundaries, adopted targets and illustrative examples explicitly. |
| Procedure         | Who runs this task and how do they know it succeeded?                | Entry conditions, prerequisites, ordered actions, checks and recovery.                                                                    |
| Policy (optional) | Who may authorize this action or grant an exception?                 | Shared restrictions, exception authority and reopening conditions, when governed independently of any one procedure.                      |

A table of configuration names, consumers and missing-value behavior can be a
single Specification when the reader needs those facts together.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD give each living page one primary type, a meaningful title and a short discovery description.
- SHOULD adopt the engineering vocabulary for a new bundle and preserve established project types and topic directories where readers or tools depend on them.

### Review the declared type

For each path in the validator's type list, write down the reader's question,
the claim this page owns and why the declared type helps the reader find that
claim. If answering requires several independent claims, identify the passages
and their owners. A project-specific name fits when readers use it for one
recognizable purpose and the page is maintained for that purpose.

Try the [type-review example](../assets/type-review-example/index.md). Both
pages have valid type strings. An editor reading their content should reach
these decisions:

| Page                                                          | Reader's question and the claim the page owns                                                                                                        | Editorial decision                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [Notes](../assets/type-review-example/delivery-notes.md)      | How is the rate calculated? What does the API return for a zero denominator? What does the team do on Monday? Each answer can change independently.  | Flag the mixed `Description`. Put the formula in a Definition, the decimal or null return contract in a Specification, and the Monday reporting practice in a Convention. Link the pages where readers need to move between answers. |
| [Service registry](../assets/type-review-example/services.md) | Which team owns each production service today? The table owns the current service-to-team mapping and is updated as membership or ownership changes. | Accept `ServiceRegistry`. Readers can find the inventory by its established project type, and each entry answers the same question.                                                                                                  |

## The index

A scheduling index can list a Definition of retry limits beside the
Specification of what a client sees while waiting. A directory can contain
both. A root index can lead through nested indexes to either page.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD list concepts directly at the root while readers can select an answer there. Add a nested index when readers need to choose among a subject's subquestions. OKF permits a directory without an index.
- SHOULD link a subject index from its parent, state its scope and give each locally owned decision a descriptive route there. A caller with a specific question can link straight to the owning section.
- SHOULD keep rules at their typed owner and use indexes for navigation.
- SHOULD use Markdown links for index entries so OKF consumers can traverse them offline. An HTML link that works in a browser does not establish an OKF relationship.
- SHOULD add a page only when it owns an answer.

## The glossary

The legacy flat `specs/<domain>.md` convention pairs specs with glossary domain
headings. A typed Specification elsewhere creates no obligation to coin a term.
A glossary entry can link to a full Definition and still explain enough for a
reader to understand the word in context.

For example, **Job output** names what one Job produced, even after its record
is gone. Three near-misses narrow or shift that meaning:

| Candidate      | Likely interpretation       | Where it misleads                                          |
| -------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Output record  | A record that holds output  | Omits which job produced it.                               |
| Failure output | The output of a failed job  | Excludes successful jobs.                                  |
| Completed job  | An execution that has ended | Names the execution itself instead of what it left behind. |

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD capture names from code, user-visible interfaces and team usage. Choose a new name whose ordinary meaning fits the concept. A plausible near-match hides the need to look it up.
- SHOULD use an optional cross-subject glossary for active aliases, UI labels and ambiguous terms. Give the minimum distinction, usually one to three sentences, and link to its owning section. Keep calculations, exceptions, procedures and guarantees at that owner.
- SHOULD explain a specialist term where its subject uses it. Group specialist terms in a subject-local Definition when readers consult them together.
- MUST account for every active alias and unique distinction when shortening a glossary, including meanings embedded in paragraphs. Move the distinction to an owner, retain a short finder or document the evidence for retirement in the change review.
- MUST preserve active spellings and disambiguation. Settle old grouping, presentation and heading compatibility [per route](./cross-references.md#preserve-the-reading-route).

## Diagrams

A state-transition diagram explains an observable contract. A diagram of the
producer and worker explains which component owns a transition.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD keep a diagram beside the claim it explains.
- MUST ship linked images with the bundle when readers need them offline.

client receiving a missing field encounters a contract violation. A reviewer
checking directory layout is applying a Convention, even if a linter enforces

- SHOULD place an observable guarantee in its Specification and a team's choice among conforming practices in its Convention.

A release operator activates a rollout. A device operator checks the
installation and restores service if verification fails. Both procedures can
depend on the same permission to release. When one operator carries out a
single task, a locally scoped permission check can fit directly in its steps.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD extract a Policy when several entry points depend on a permission rule that changes independently.

- MUST NOT invent an approver or independent permission rule to populate a type.

## Contributor routes

A contributor guide can direct a new maintainer to the setup procedure and a
reviewer to the same convention used by the linter. Each route leads to one
maintained rule.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD document each subject's scope and its nearest confusing neighbor. Give a tie-breaker a contributor can apply to a new claim and explain when to add a subject. For instance, a worker-pool cap belongs with dispatch internals unless it promises an outcome to callers.
- SHOULD link the placement convention from durable human and agent entry points and update it when responsibility moves. Link editable callers directly to their governing section.

2	
3	## Check the whole documentation root
4	
5	Run `check-docs.mjs` on first adoption, during migration and after editing a
6	bundle. It inventories visible Markdown even if every living page is untyped.
7	In a populated directory without a root index it reports the missing
8	`index.md` and continues checking the available pages and links.
9	
10	### Prepare the installed skill
11	
12	Set `skill_dir` to the installed skill directory. Use Node, npm and a Python 3
13	environment with PyYAML. For example, from the project root on a POSIX shell:
14	
15	```bash
16	skill_dir=.agents/skills/living-project-documentation
17	npm ci --prefix "$skill_dir/scripts" --ignore-scripts
18	python3 -m venv .venv-okf
19	. .venv-okf/bin/activate
20	python3 -m pip install PyYAML==6.0.3
21	validator="$VIRTUAL_ENV/validate-okf-v0.3.py"
22	curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/skills/okf-generate/scripts/validate.py -o "$validator"
23	```
24	
25	The command verifies the pinned validator's SHA-256 before invoking Python.
26	After setup the check runs offline. You can also point `--validator` at the
27	same file in a local [OKF v0.3 checkout](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/skills/okf-generate/scripts/validate.py).
28	
29	### Run and interpret the check
30	
31	```bash
32	node "$skill_dir/scripts/check-docs.mjs" --validator "$validator" docs
33	```
34	
35	The exit status is **0** when the required checks pass, **1** for findings
36	that require a fix, and **2** when a setup, invocation or execution problem
37	prevents a complete check. Use the diagnostics to locate each finding:
38	
39	- **Required by OKF.** A format error such as frontmatter on a nested `index.md` (`E004`) or on a `log.md` (`E006`) fails the check.
40	- **Required by this skill.** A living page needs a nonempty string `type`, a route from the root index and resolvable local links and fragments. OKF permits untyped Markdown and emits `W120`. The engineering check determines the type using the YAML 1.2 core schema. For example, an unquoted `type: On` is a string under that schema. The pinned Python parser can still emit `W120` for it. Quoting `"On"` makes both parsers read the same type.
41	- **Recommendations.** Upstream warnings remain visible. For example, a root index without a version declaration can receive `W125`. Check for an accompanying required finding before deciding what to fix.
42	- **Editorial review.** The report lists typed pages on both passing and failing runs. For each page, use its reader's question and the claim it owns to [review the declared type](./documentation-structure.md#review-the-declared-type). Root reachability and fragment resolution can pass even when a subject index omits a decision, a valid heading answers another question or a runbook sends a reader through an unrelated guide. [Trace each affected reader's route](./consulting-and-upkeep.md#verify-a-readers-route) to judge the answer and its limits.
43	
44	For checkout links to neighboring files, add `--source-root .` from the
45	repository root. For immutable Markdown evidence, name each original by its
46	exact bundle-relative path. A reachable companion can cite the source in its
47	body or a local `sources[].resource` field.
48	
49	```bash
50	node "$skill_dir/scripts/check-docs.mjs" --validator "$validator" --source-root . \
51	  --evidence evidence/accepted.md --evidence evidence/incident.md docs
52	```
53	
54	**Guidelines:**
55	
56	- MUST run the whole-root check when determining whether a tree meets the required format and engineering rules.
57	- MUST verify each named source against its companion and original bytes. Its expected `W120` stays in the report. An additional untyped living page or a separate error on the named source still fails.
58	
59	## Focused checks
60	
61	The individual Node commands default to `./docs` and accept another directory
62	as a positional argument. They retain their existing root-index and OKF
63	detection for callers using them during a targeted edit.
64	
65	| Command                | Question                                                                                                                                           |
66	| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

# Validators

## Check the whole documentation root

Run `check-docs.mjs` on first adoption, during migration and after editing a
bundle. It inventories visible Markdown even if every living page is untyped.
In a populated directory without a root index it reports the missing
`index.md` and continues checking the available pages and links.

### Prepare the installed skill

Set `skill_dir` to the installed skill directory. Use Node, npm and a Python 3
environment with PyYAML. For example, from the project root on a POSIX shell:

```bash
skill_dir=.agents/skills/living-project-documentation
npm ci --prefix "$skill_dir/scripts" --ignore-scripts
python3 -m venv .venv-okf
. .venv-okf/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install PyYAML==6.0.3
validator="$VIRTUAL_ENV/validate-okf-v0.3.py"
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/skills/okf-generate/scripts/validate.py -o "$validator"
```

The command verifies the pinned validator's SHA-256 before invoking Python.
After setup the check runs offline. You can also point `--validator` at the
same file in a local [OKF v0.3 checkout](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/skills/okf-generate/scripts/validate.py).

### Run and interpret the check

```bash
node "$skill_dir/scripts/check-docs.mjs" --validator "$validator" docs
```

The exit status is **0** when the required checks pass, **1** for findings
that require a fix, and **2** when a setup, invocation or execution problem
prevents a complete check. Use the diagnostics to locate each finding:

- **Required by OKF.** A format error such as frontmatter on a nested `index.md` (`E004`) or on a `log.md` (`E006`) fails the check.
- **Required by this skill.** A living page needs a nonempty string `type`, a route from the root index and resolvable local links and fragments. OKF permits untyped Markdown and emits `W120`. The engineering check determines the type using the YAML 1.2 core schema. For example, an unquoted `type: On` is a string under that schema. The pinned Python parser can still emit `W120` for it. Quoting `"On"` makes both parsers read the same type.
- **Recommendations.** Upstream warnings remain visible. For example, a root index without a version declaration can receive `W125`. Check for an accompanying required finding before deciding what to fix.
- **Editorial review.** The report lists typed pages on both passing and failing runs. For each page, use its reader's question and the claim it owns to [review the declared type](./documentation-structure.md#review-the-declared-type). Root reachability and fragment resolution can pass even when a subject index omits a decision, a valid heading answers another question or a runbook sends a reader through an unrelated guide. [Trace each affected reader's route](./consulting-and-upkeep.md#verify-a-readers-route) to judge the answer and its limits.

For checkout links to neighboring files, add `--source-root .` from the
repository root. For immutable Markdown evidence, name each original by its
exact bundle-relative path. A reachable companion can cite the source in its
body or a local `sources[].resource` field.

```bash
node "$skill_dir/scripts/check-docs.mjs" --validator "$validator" --source-root . \
  --evidence evidence/accepted.md --evidence evidence/incident.md docs
```

**Guidelines:**

- MUST run the whole-root check when determining whether a tree meets the required format and engineering rules.
- MUST verify each named source against its companion and original bytes. Its expected `W120` stays in the report. An additional untyped living page or a separate error on the named source still fails.

## Focused checks

The individual Node commands default to `./docs` and accept another directory
as a positional argument. They retain their existing root-index and OKF
detection for callers using them during a targeted edit.

| Command                | Question                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `check-index.mjs`      | Can a reader reach every page from the root index? An OKF route may pass through nested indexes. The legacy layout lists pages directly.           |
| `check-references.mjs` | Do local Markdown links, fragments and OKF path fields resolve? The local checker also checks rendered HTML links and images for export usability. |
| `check-glossary.mjs`   | Does each legacy flat spec have a matching glossary heading? OKF type names do not imply a glossary pairing.                                       |

## Check the export independently

Run the whole-root command on the exported directory outside the checkout.
Leave out `--source-root` so the check sees only the files a recipient gets.
Pass the same evidence paths used for the checkout.

**Guidelines:**

- MUST run project gates in the checkout and the whole-root check on both source and export.
- MUST include all distributed evidence and linked assets in the export and compare their hashes with the originals.
- MUST trace an index route and a moved fragment offline, and resolve each external source against its published location or pinned revision.

2	
3	Operational notes on what happens after a post is published — the part that
4	doesn't belong in a code comment because it spans two files (`server/app.ts`
5	and `server/deploy-hook.ts`) and one decision worth explaining once rather
6	than re-deriving at either call site.

8	## What publishing actually does
9	
10	Publishing a post is three steps, in order:
11	
12	1. Write a `revisions` row — a snapshot of the post's title and body at the
13	   moment of publish.
14	2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
15	3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.
16	
17	The first two are a single logical write and either both happen or neither
18	does. The third is best-effort: a site's deploy hook is usually a webhook on
19	someone else's static host (Vercel, Netlify, and similar all expose one), and
20	those are occasionally slow or briefly unavailable — worth a retry, not worth
21	losing the author's published content over.
22	
23	## Why a failed deploy hook doesn't fail the publish
24	
25	By the time `triggerDeployHook` runs, the post and its revision are already
26	committed. Rolling that back because a webhook timed out would throw away
27	real work over a problem that's usually transient and, worse, outside this
28	app's control entirely. Instead, the publish response carries
29	`deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor shows the author which case they're
30	in — see `PostEditorPage.tsx`'s toast copy.
31	
32	## The retry policy
33	
34	Three attempts, with a linear backoff between them. That's tuned for "a cold
35	serverless function taking a moment to wake up," not for a target that's
36	genuinely down — three attempts a few hundred milliseconds apart won't save a
37	publish from a deploy hook that's been deleted or misconfigured. When every
38	attempt fails, `deploy-hook.ts` logs the exhaustion at `error` (there's no
39	error tracker on the API side to hand it to instead — see `shared/logger.ts`)
40	and returns `{ ok: false }` rather than throwing, so the route above always
41	gets a definite answer either way.
42	
43	## Rolling back a bad publish
44	
45	There's no unpublish button in this cut of the product. The revision a
46	publish writes is a record of what went out, not an undo mechanism —
47	reverting live content means editing the post back to the previous
48	revision's text and publishing again.

## Why a failed deploy hook doesn't fail the publish

By the time `triggerDeployHook` runs, the post and its revision are already
committed. Rolling that back because a webhook timed out would throw away
real work over a problem that's usually transient and, worse, outside this
app's control entirely. Instead, the publish response carries
`deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor shows the author which case they're
in — see `PostEditorPage.tsx`'s toast copy.

## The retry policy

Three attempts, with a linear backoff between them. That's tuned for "a cold
serverless function taking a moment to wake up," not for a target that's
genuinely down — three attempts a few hundred milliseconds apart won't save a
publish from a deploy hook that's been deleted or misconfigured. When every
attempt fails, `deploy-hook.ts` logs the exhaustion at `error` (there's no
error tracker on the API side to hand it to instead — see `shared/logger.ts`)
and returns `{ ok: false }` rather than throwing, so the route above always
gets a definite answer either way.

## Rolling back a bad publish

There's no unpublish button in this cut of the product. The revision a
publish writes is a record of what went out, not an undo mechanism —
reverting live content means editing the post back to the previous
revision's text and publishing again.

contract, while the operator can change the release check independently.

# Deployment

The release operator uses a checkout of the release revision with production
deployment access. Only the release operator may deploy or roll back, even when
someone else has credentials that can run the command. Before release, record
the previous revision for rollback.

## Releasing

```bash
npm run build
npm run migrate:up -- --env production
npm run deploy
```

Migrations MUST run before the deploy, never after. The new code assumes the new
schema and the old code tolerates it, because every migration here is written to be
safe against the version already running. Deploying first inverts that and opens a
window where live code queries columns that do not exist yet.

The worker package deploys from the same command and the same commit. It MUST NOT be
deployed on its own to pick up a fix: the two packages share `shared/`, and a split
deploy runs two versions of it against one queue.

## Verifying a release

The deploy is not finished when the command returns. Watch the worker's claim rate for
five minutes and confirm queued jobs are being claimed. A release that broke the
queue consumer can deploy cleanly and stop claiming while requests still succeed.

Queued jobs include those [waiting for a retry](../scheduling/outcomes.md#attempts-and-retries).
Check the claim rate before treating a queued job as evidence of a stalled worker.

## Rolling back

As release operator, first check whether a destructive contract migration
already removed data. If it
did, stop and hand the restore to the on-call operator. Deploying an older
revision cannot bring the data back.

For a code rollback, use the recorded previous revision that works with the
current schema:

```bash
npm run deploy -- --revision <previous>
```

Leave the migration in place. Destructive changes have separate expand and
contract migrations so the earlier code can run against the expanded schema.
Roll back to the revision before the contract and correct the schema with a
forward migration.

8	
9	How someone finds out what happened. This domain covers the rules that turn an
10	outcome into a message, the channels those messages reach, and the digest that
11	collapses a run of them.
12	
13	## Rules
14	
15	A **Notification Rule** belongs to the account, not to a template, and selects the jobs it
16	cares about by template name and terminal state. Two rules matching the same job both
17	fire; the product does not deduplicate across rules, because each names its own
18	channel and suppressing one would silently drop a recipient.

21	rule can select, so a job that never finishes never notifies —
22	see [which states are terminal, including cancellation with retries left](./scheduling/outcomes.md#states).

25	
26	A **Channel** is an email address, webhook, or chat integration. A rule names
27	exactly one channel. A channel serves many rules, so disabling a channel
28	silences every rule pointing at it at once, and the rules stay enabled rather than

32	that fails is recorded against the channel and visible in its history; the product

34	an operator who has already moved on.

39	message for all matching outcomes in that interval. An interval that matched nothing emits

44	the message links each job instead, so a digest stays the same size whatever ran.

47	
48	A notification is not an acknowledgement. There is no acknowledge, snooze, or
49	escalate, and nothing changes state because a message was read — the product reports
50	outcomes and leaves the response to whoever receives it.

A **Channel** is an email address, webhook, or chat integration. A rule names
exactly one channel. A channel serves many rules, so disabling a channel
silences every rule pointing at it at once, and the rules stay enabled rather than
being rewritten.

that fails is recorded against the channel and visible in its history; the product

A **Digest** collects outcomes on a fixed interval. The rule emits one

A notification is not an acknowledgement. There is no acknowledge, snooze, or
escalate, and nothing changes state because a message was read — the product reports
outcomes and leaves the response to whoever receives it.

# Job creation and history

## Templates and schedules

A **Job Template** carries a name, the work to run, and an optional schedule. The name is
unique across the account and is what job history is grouped by, so renaming a
template regroups every job it has already produced.

A **Schedule** is the recurrence attached to a template. It produces one job
each time it fires, evaluated in UTC. If the previous job is still running,
the schedule creates a second job. The two can run concurrently within the
worker pool limit. A template with no schedule produces jobs only when someone runs it by hand.

A template is enabled or disabled. A disabled template's schedule does not fire and it
cannot be run by hand, but disabling does not touch jobs already created — a job
queued a moment earlier is still claimed and still runs.

Editing a template does not change jobs already created: each job carries a copy of
the work it was created with, so a template edited while a job is queued runs the old
definition once more.

## Creating a job

A run creates a job, one execution of a template. A firing schedule and a manual
run produce the same record. Only the job's `trigger` field distinguishes them.

A run returns a queued job. A saturated pool can delay its start indefinitely.
A repeated worker claim cannot start a second copy of that job. The
[dispatch boundary](./dispatch.md) explains how all producers share capacity.
See [job outcomes](./outcomes.md#states) for the states a caller can observe.

## Output and pruning

A job's record is pruned thirty days after it ends. Its job output outlives the record
and is addressed by the job's identifier, so a link to output written last quarter
still resolves once the job it came from is gone. Earlier attempts' output is
pruned with the record.

## What scheduling does not do

A job does not trigger another job. There is no dependency graph, no fan-out, and no
"run this once that succeeds" — a template needing a second step runs it inside its
own work.

5	---
6	
7	# Directory Structure
8	
9	The API and worker are the two deployable **Packages**. Each runs in its own
10	environment. This convention governs the modules each package contains or imports.
11	
12	The general discipline — put shared logic at the lowest tier with more than one
13	caller, name a file for what it holds — belongs to the installed code-maintainability
14	capability. What follows is this repository's own tiers and paths, which nothing
15	outside it could infer.
16	
17	## The Tree
18	
19	```text
20	<root>
21	├── api/                       # the API package: creates jobs, serves the dashboard
22	│   ├── routes/<route>/
23	│   │   ├── _components/       # used by this route only
24	│   │   └── handler.ts
25	│   └── _/                     # feature-agnostic modules shared across routes
26	├── worker/                    # the worker package: claims jobs, runs attempts
27	└── shared/                    # the few modules both packages import
28	```
29	
30	## Tiers
31	
32	A module sits at the lowest tier that has more than one caller, and MUST NOT be
33	promoted in anticipation of a second — a module promoted early is one every package
34	pays to read while one of them uses it.
35	
36	`shared/` MUST stay deliberate. A module there is imported by two deployables that
37	run in separate processes, so a change to it changes both at once. It belongs there only
38	when both packages need the same _behaviour_, never merely the same shape.
39	
40	The import direction is one-way: `api/` and `worker/` MAY import `shared/`; `shared/`
41	MUST NOT import either, and the two packages MUST NOT import each other. Each
42	production package contains only its own modules and shared dependencies. A
43	cross-package import can compile in the checkout and fail in the deployed process.
44	
45	## Naming

---
type: Convention
title: Directory structure
description: Module placement, import direction and route naming for the API and worker.
---

# Directory Structure

The API and worker are the two deployable **Packages**. Each runs in its own
environment. This convention governs the modules each package contains or imports.

The general discipline — put shared logic at the lowest tier with more than one
caller, name a file for what it holds — belongs to the installed code-maintainability
capability. What follows is this repository's own tiers and paths, which nothing
outside it could infer.

## The Tree

```text
<root>
├── api/                       # the API package: creates jobs, serves the dashboard
│   ├── routes/<route>/
│   │   ├── _components/       # used by this route only
│   │   └── handler.ts
│   └── _/                     # feature-agnostic modules shared across routes
├── worker/                    # the worker package: claims jobs, runs attempts
└── shared/                    # the few modules both packages import
```

## Tiers

A module sits at the lowest tier that has more than one caller, and MUST NOT be
promoted in anticipation of a second — a module promoted early is one every package
pays to read while one of them uses it.

`shared/` MUST stay deliberate. A module there is imported by two deployables that
run in separate processes, so a change to it changes both at once. It belongs there only
when both packages need the same _behaviour_, never merely the same shape.

The import direction is one-way: `api/` and `worker/` MAY import `shared/`; `shared/`
MUST NOT import either, and the two packages MUST NOT import each other. Each
production package contains only its own modules and shared dependencies. A
cross-package import can compile in the checkout and fail in the deployed process.

## Naming

A file is named for what it holds, in kebab-case; a directory, for the thing its files
are about. A route directory MUST match the URL segment it serves — the router derives
one from the other, so a mismatch is a 404 nobody can see in review.

`_`-prefixed directories are not routed. Anything under `routes/` without the prefix
becomes a URL, so a helper dropped there unprefixed is published.

description: What a publish writes, the deploy-hook contract an author sees, the retry policy, and why there's no in-app undo.
---

# Publishing

Publishing a post is three steps, in order:

1. Write a `revisions` row — a snapshot of the post's title and body at the
   moment of publish.
2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.

The first two are one transaction: either both happen or neither does. The
third is best-effort. A site's deploy hook is usually a webhook on someone
else's static host (Vercel, Netlify and similar all expose one), and those
are occasionally slow or briefly unavailable — worth a retry, not worth
losing the author's published content over.

## What a failed hook does and doesn't do

By the time the hook call runs, the post and its revision are already
committed. A failed hook never undoes either: the post stays `published` and
its revision stays recorded even when every retry fails. See
[what the Revisions screen shows for a publish like this](./revisions.md#publishing-and-a-failed-hook).

The publish response carries `deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor
shows the author which case they're in rather than pretending publish either
fully succeeded or fully failed.

## Retry policy

The hook gets three attempts, with a linear backoff between them (250ms,
then 500ms). That's tuned for a cold serverless function taking a moment to
wake up, not for a target that's genuinely down — three attempts a few
hundred milliseconds apart won't save a publish from a deploy hook that's
been deleted or misconfigured. When every attempt fails, the API logs the
exhaustion at `error` and returns `deployTriggered: false` rather than
throwing, so the route above always gets a definite answer either way.

This app makes no promise about how long after a successful hook call the
site itself goes live — that's the host's own build pipeline, which this app
has no visibility into and no control over.

## There is no unpublish

There's no unpublish action in this cut of the product. The revision a
publish writes is a record of what went out, not an undo mechanism:
reverting live content means editing the post back to the previous
revision's text and publishing again, which writes a new revision rather
than erasing the old one.

# Revisions

The Revisions screen lists every revision for a site, grouped by the post
each one belongs to. Each group's heading uses the post's current title;
each row uses the title that was saved at the moment of that publish, so
renaming a post afterward doesn't rewrite what an older row says it
published.

A draft save updates the post without writing a revision. Only a publish
adds one.

## Ordering

Revisions are listed newest first within a post. Two publishes in the same
second are ordinary — the API breaks the tie by revision id, descending, so
the more recently written revision still sorts first even when its
timestamp exactly matches an earlier one.

## Publishing and a failed hook

A post becomes `published` together with the revision that snapshots it, in
one transaction. A failed deploy hook doesn't touch either: the post stays
published and its revision stays in place even when the site itself didn't
rebuild. See [the publish contract and what a failed hook means](./publishing.md#what-a-failed-hook-does-and-doesnt-do)
and [recovering a missed build](./guides/desk.md).

# AGENTS.md

## What this project is

A small hosted CMS. An author signs in — session handling lives outside this
cut of the product, so there's no sign-in screen here and the API reads who
the author is from what the session boundary forwards — and manages one or
more customer sites from the same account. Each site has its own posts;
opening a post gives you a full-page editor with a title, a body, a draft
save, and a publish action. Publishing snapshots the post into a revision and
calls the site's deploy hook so the static build actually goes out.

The sidebar carries two sections, Posts and Revisions, and shows which author
is signed in underneath them. There's no dashboard, no settings page, and no
onboarding flow yet.

## How the code is organized

`src/` is the SPA: `routes/` holds the three real screens (a per-site post
list, the post editor, and that site's revision history) plus the shell they
render inside, `components/` holds
what's reusable across more than one of them, `lib/` is where a cross-cutting
concern — the API client, the query client, consent, analytics — gets exactly
one home, and `queries/` holds the TanStack Query option factories, one
export per file, grouped by the resource they read or write rather than by
the screen that happens to call them first.

generated SQL migrations under `db/`, and the deploy-hook call in its own
module because it's the one thing in this app that talks to somebody else's
infrastructure and needed a retry policy to go with it.

`shared/` is the one thing both sides import — right now just the logger.
Anything that earns a place there has to make sense with zero DOM APIs and
zero Node APIs in scope, since it's bundled into the browser build and run
directly by the API both.

side.

## How changes are made

Nothing lands on `main` directly. Sketch the change and get it agreed on
before writing it — a plan is a much cheaper place to catch a misunderstood
requirement than a finished diff is. A pull request gets reviewed by someone
other than whoever wrote it, and it merges once that review has nothing left
to raise and the checks in `README.md` are green.

The [maintenance decisions](maintenance/decisions.md) record agreed work.

Keep a pull request to the problem it set out to solve. Renaming something
you noticed in passing, reformatting a file you didn't otherwise touch, or
folding in an unrelated fix makes the diff harder to review for the same
reason it was harder to write: two changes being reasoned about as though
they were one. Split it, or leave the rest for its own change.

## Publishing, briefly

Publish does three things, in order: write a revision snapshot of the post's
current title and body, flip the post to `published`, and call the site's
deploy hook. The first two are one transaction; the third is best-effort — a
site's deploy hook lives on somebody else's infrastructure, and a slow or
briefly-down webhook shouldn't cost the author their published content. The
API reports whether the deploy actually fired (`deployTriggered`) and the
editor tells the author which case they're in, rather than pretending publish
either fully succeeded or fully failed. `docs/deploy-hooks.md` has the retry
policy and the reasoning behind it; read it before changing
`server/deploy-hook.ts` or the publish route that calls it.

The revision written by step one is what the Revisions screen reads back, so
a change to what publish snapshots changes what that screen shows.
